title: Biochemistry
standard_text: The structure and function of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids; functional groups; dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis; enzymes and the factors that affect them; and the structure of the cell membrane and transport across it. (summary of The Ontario Curriculum, Grades 11 and 12: Science (2008), Biology, Grade 12, University Preparation (SBI4U), Strand B: Biochemistry)
meta_desc: Free Grade 12 Biology (SBI4U) worksheets on biochemistry: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids, functional groups, enzymes, the fluid mosaic model and membrane transport. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Large biological molecules are built by dehydration synthesis and broken by hydrolysis.
key_sub: Enzymes lower the activation energy and are specific to their substrate.
body_html:
How to think about it

The four groups of macromolecules are carbohydrates (monosaccharides such as glucose), lipids (fatty acids and glycerol), proteins (amino acids joined by peptide bonds) and nucleic acids (nucleotides). Joining monomers releases water (dehydration synthesis); breaking them apart uses water (hydrolysis).

An enzyme's active site fits its substrate. High temperature or the wrong pH changes its shape (denaturation). The cell membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with proteins (the fluid mosaic model); small non-polar molecules diffuse through it, while ions need channels or pumps.

Example

How many water molecules are released when 4 glucose molecules join in a chain?

Each new bond releases one water molecule.

Answer: 3

Example

Why does an enzyme stop working at 70 °C?

Heat breaks the bonds that hold its shape.

Answer: it is denatured: the active site changes shape

Common mistakes

  • Saying enzymes are used up in a reaction.
  • Thinking denaturation means the enzyme is killed: proteins are not alive.
  • Mixing up active transport (uses ATP) and facilitated diffusion (no ATP).

A molecule that fits the active site and blocks the substrate.

items.q: Which bond holds the primary structure of a protein together?
items.e: The sequence of amino acids.

items.q: Glucose has M<sub>r</sub> 180 and water 18. Calculate the M<sub>r</sub> of a straight chain of 6 glucose units joined by condensation.
Glucose has M<sub>r</sub> 180 and water 18. Calculate the M<sub>r</sub> of a straight chain of 8 glucose units joined by condensation.
Why is ATP a good immediate energy source?
c: hydrolysis releases a small, manageable amount of energy in one step
it stores a large amount of energy
items.e: ATP → ADP + Pᵢ.

items.q: Why is glycogen well suited to energy storage in animals?
c: it is highly branched, so glucose is released quickly
items.e: Enzymes act on the many branch ends.

items.q: Glycerol has M<sub>r</sub> 92 and a fatty acid has M<sub>r</sub> 280. Calculate the M<sub>r</sub> of the triglyceride made from glycerol and three of these fatty acids (water M<sub>r</sub> 18).
items.e: Three ester bonds form, releasing 3 water molecules: 92 + 3 × 280 − 3 × 18 = 878.

items.q: Which group is on every amino acid?
c: an amine group and a carboxyl group
items.e: The R group is different for each.

items.q: Glycine (M<sub>r</sub> 75) and glutamine (M<sub>r</sub> 146) join to make a dipeptide. Calculate the M<sub>r</sub> of the dipeptide.
items.e: Condensation releases one water molecule: 75 + 146 − 18 = 203.

items.q: What is the primary structure of a protein?
items.e: It is read from the N-terminal end.

items.q: Glucose has M<sub>r</sub> 180 and water 18. Calculate the M<sub>r</sub> of a straight chain of 10 glucose units joined by condensation.
What is ATP made of?
c: adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups
items.e: ATP is a nucleotide derivative.

items.q: What do hydrogen ions affect in the body?
c: the speed of nerve impulses only
items.e: Enzymes work best at their optimum pH.

items.q: What bond joins nucleotides in a polynucleotide?
items.e: Between the phosphate of one and the sugar of the next.

items.q: Which disaccharide is made from glucose and fructose?
items.e: Lactose is glucose + galactose; maltose is glucose + glucose.

items.q: Which bond joins nucleotides in a nucleic acid?
items.e: It links the sugar of one nucleotide to the phosphate of the next.

items.q: How many peptide bonds are in a single polypeptide chain of 20 amino acids?
items.e: A chain of n amino acids has n − 1 peptide bonds: 19.

items.q: Which is a saturated fatty acid?
items.e: It has no C=C double bonds.

items.q: What is the most abundant protein in animals?
items.e: RuBisCO is the most abundant protein in the biosphere.

items.q: Which polysaccharide is a branched storage form in animals?
items.e: It is stored in liver and muscle.

items.q: Which bond joins monosaccharides in a polysaccharide?
items.e: It forms by dehydration.

items.q: How many peptide bonds are in a single polypeptide chain of 50 amino acids?
items.e: A chain of n amino acids has n − 1 peptide bonds: 49.

items.q: A starch solution takes 40 s to be broken down by amylase. Calculate the rate as 1/time.
In the DNA of a bacterium, 14% of the bases are adenine. What percentage are adenine and thymine together?
In the DNA of a fungus, 28% of the bases are adenine. What percentage are guanine?
items.e: A + T = 56%, so G + C = 44%, and guanine = half of that: 22.0%.

items.q: Lysine (M<sub>r</sub> 146) and glutamine (M<sub>r</sub> 146) join to make a dipeptide. Calculate the M<sub>r</sub> of the dipeptide.
items.e: Condensation releases one water molecule: 146 + 146 − 18 = 274.

items.q: How many water molecules are released when 200 glucose molecules join to form a polysaccharide chain?
items.e: Each glycosidic bond releases one water molecule, and 200 monomers make 199 bonds: 199.

items.q: How many water molecules are released when 12 glucose molecules join to form a polysaccharide chain?
items.e: Each glycosidic bond releases one water molecule, and 12 monomers make 11 bonds: 11.

items.q: Which is an example of a competitive inhibitor in medicine?
c: a drug with a similar shape to the substrate
items.e: It competes for the active site.

items.q: In the DNA of an insect, 24% of the bases are adenine. What percentage are adenine and thymine together?
Why does a change in pH affect enzyme activity?
c: it changes the charges on R groups, breaking ionic and hydrogen bonds
it gives molecules more kinetic energy
it adds water to the enzyme
items.e: The active site shape changes.

items.q: How does a competitive inhibitor work?
c: it binds to the active site, so substrate cannot bind
it binds elsewhere and changes the active site shape
items.e: Adding more substrate reduces its effect.

items.q: Which turns blue-black with iodine?
items.e: Iodine sits inside the starch helix.

items.q: Catalase releases 4.0 mL of oxygen in the first 180 s. Calculate the mean rate in mL per minute.
How does a non-competitive inhibitor work?
c: it binds to the active site
it binds away from the active site and changes its shape
it raises the activation energy only
items.e: More substrate does not reduce its effect.

items.q: Which polysaccharide forms the exoskeleton of arthropods?
items.e: It is a complex polysaccharide with nitrogen.

items.q: A starch solution takes 50 s to be broken down by amylase. Calculate the rate as 1/time.
What is the effect of a cofactor such as chloride ions on amylase?
c: it helps the enzyme work or bind its substrate
items.e: Many enzymes need cofactors.

items.q: Why does a high temperature stop an enzyme working?
c: hydrogen and ionic bonds break and the active site changes shape (denatures)
items.e: The substrate no longer fits.

items.q: Alanine (M<sub>r</sub> 89) and alanine (M<sub>r</sub> 89) join to make a dipeptide. Calculate the M<sub>r</sub> of the dipeptide.
items.e: Condensation releases one water molecule: 89 + 89 − 18 = 160.

items.q: How many water molecules are released when 6 glucose molecules join to form a polysaccharide chain?
items.e: Each glycosidic bond releases one water molecule, and 6 monomers make 5 bonds: 5.

items.q: Which class of enzymes is responsible for transferring a group from one substrate to another?
items.e: Transferases: transferring a group from one substrate to another.

items.q: What does quaternary structure describe?
c: more than one polypeptide chain joined together
items.e: Haemoglobin has four chains.

items.q: How do you test for a non-reducing sugar such as sucrose?
c: boil with dilute HCl, neutralize, then do the Benedict's test
items.e: The acid hydrolyzes sucrose into reducing sugars.

items.q: A starch solution takes 160 s to be broken down by amylase. Calculate the rate as 1/time.
A starch solution takes 200 s to be broken down by amylase. Calculate the rate as 1/time.
What do ligases do?
c: transferring a group from one substrate to another
removing groups without hydrolysis, leaving double bonds
joining two compounds together, such as C–O or C–N bonds
items.e: Ligases: joining two compounds together, such as C–O or C–N bonds.

items.q: Which food is likely to give a positive iodine test?
items.e: Potatoes store starch.

items.q: Why must the Benedict's test be heated?
c: the reaction needs heat to reduce the copper(II) ions
items.e: Use a water bath at about 80 °C or above.

items.q: What do isomerases do?
c: joining two compounds together, such as C–O or C–N bonds
removing groups without hydrolysis, leaving double bonds
catalyzing oxidation and reduction between two substrates
items.e: Isomerases: converting one isomer into another.

items.q: At 25 °C the initial rate of an enzyme reaction is 20 units and at 35 °C it is 35 units. Calculate the percentage increase in rate.
Which class of enzymes is responsible for catalyzing oxidation and reduction between two substrates?
items.e: Oxidoreductases: catalyzing oxidation and reduction between two substrates.

items.q: Which test shows protein?
c: add biuret reagent: blue to purple
items.e: Biuret reacts with peptide bonds.

items.q: Which test shows starch?
c: add iodine solution: orange-brown to blue-black
items.e: Iodine fits inside the amylose helix.

items.q: Which class of enzymes is responsible for joining two compounds together, such as C–O or C–N bonds?
items.e: Ligases: joining two compounds together, such as C–O or C–N bonds.

items.q: What does DNA polymerase do?
c: joins new nucleotides to form phosphodiester bonds
items.e: It works in the 5′ to 3′ direction.

items.q: What is hem in hemoglobin an example of?
items.e: Haem in hemoglobin: a prosthetic group.

items.q: What is NAD and NADP an example of?
items.e: NAD and NADP: coenzymes.

items.q: What do oxidoreductases do?
c: removing groups without hydrolysis, leaving double bonds
joining two compounds together, such as C–O or C–N bonds
catalyzing oxidation and reduction between two substrates
items.e: Oxidoreductases: catalyzing oxidation and reduction between two substrates.

items.q: What do lyases do?
c: removing groups without hydrolysis, leaving double bonds
transferring a group from one substrate to another
joining two compounds together, such as C–O or C–N bonds
items.e: Lyases: removing groups without hydrolysis, leaving double bonds.

items.q: Why does water have a high specific heat capacity?
c: lots of energy is needed to break the hydrogen bonds
it has covalent bonds between molecules
items.e: It buffers temperature changes.

items.q: 13 glucose molecules join by dehydration synthesis to form a starch chain. How many water molecules are released?
items.e: One water per bond: 13 − 1 = 12.

items.q: How many bonds join 28 amino acids in one straight chain?
items.e: A chain of 28 units has 27 links.

items.q: Which kind of macromolecule is butter?
items.e: Butter is one of the lipids.

items.q: Which kind of macromolecule is DNA?
items.e: DNA is one of the nucleic acids.

items.q: Many fatty acids and glycerol join to form which kind of molecule?
items.e: fatty acids and glycerol → lipids.

items.q: 38 glucose molecules join by dehydration synthesis to form a starch chain. How many water molecules are released?
items.e: One water per bond: 38 − 1 = 37.

items.q: Which kind of macromolecule is olive oil?
items.e: Olive oil is one of the lipids.

items.q: 42 amino acids join by dehydration synthesis to form a protein chain. How many water molecules are released?
items.e: One water per bond: 42 − 1 = 41.

items.q: Many monosaccharides (simple sugars like glucose) join to form which kind of molecule?
items.e: monosaccharides (simple sugars like glucose) → carbohydrates.

items.q: How many bonds join 60 nucleotides in one straight chain?
items.e: A chain of 60 units has 59 links.

items.q: What are the building blocks (monomers) of carbohydrates?
items.e: Carbohydrates are built from monosaccharides (simple sugars like glucose).

items.q: Which kind of macromolecule is an enzyme such as amylase?
items.e: An enzyme such as amylase is one of the proteins.

items.q: 60 amino acids join by dehydration synthesis to form a protein chain. How many water molecules are released?
items.e: One water per bond: 60 − 1 = 59.

items.q: What are the building blocks (monomers) of proteins?
items.e: Proteins are built from amino acids.

items.q: 33 amino acids join by dehydration synthesis to form a protein chain. How many water molecules are released?
items.e: One water per bond: 33 − 1 = 32.

items.q: How many bonds join 36 glucose molecules in one straight chain?
items.e: A chain of 36 units has 35 links.

items.q: Which kind of macromolecule is table sugar (sucrose)?
items.e: Table sugar (sucrose) is one of the carbohydrates.

items.q: Which kind of macromolecule is the phospholipids in a cell membrane?
items.e: The phospholipids in a cell membrane is one of the lipids.

items.q: What are the building blocks (monomers) of nucleic acids?
items.e: Nucleic acids are built from nucleotides.

items.q: How many bonds join 18 glucose molecules in one straight chain?
items.e: A chain of 18 units has 17 links.

items.q: A potato strip had a mass of 4.80 g. After 30 minutes in a solution its mass was 5.52 g. What is the percentage change in mass?
items.e: Percentage change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100 = 0.72 ÷ 4.80 × 100. Water entered by osmosis: the solution had a higher water potential.

items.q: What is the surface area to volume ratio of a block of agar measuring 2 cm × 3 cm × 6 cm?
items.e: Surface area = 72 cm²; volume = 36 mL; ratio = 72 ÷ 36. Smaller blocks have a larger ratio.

items.q: Cell X has a water potential of −200 kPa and cell Y has −1200 kPa. In which direction does water move by osmosis?
c: from cell X to cell Y
from cell Y to cell X
items.e: Water moves from a higher (less negative) water potential to a lower (more negative) water potential.

items.q: Cell A has a water potential of −800 kPa and cell B has −500 kPa. Which has the higher water potential?
items.e: The value closer to zero (−500 kPa) is higher.

items.q: What happens in interphase?
c: DNA replicates and the cell grows
chromosomes line up at the equator
items.e: Organelles are also copied.

items.q: A potato strip had a mass of 8.00 g. After 30 minutes in a solution its mass was 7.20 g. What is the percentage change in mass?
items.e: Percentage change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100 = −0.80 ÷ 8.00 × 100. Water left by osmosis: the solution had a lower water potential.

items.q: Which microscope has the highest resolution?
items.e: Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light.

items.e: Percentage change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100 = −0.50 ÷ 2.50 × 100. Water left by osmosis: the solution had a lower water potential.

items.q: A potato strip had a mass of 3.20 g. After 30 minutes in a solution its mass was 4.00 g. What is the percentage change in mass?
items.e: Percentage change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100 = 0.80 ÷ 3.20 × 100. Water entered by osmosis: the solution had a higher water potential.

items.q: A potato strip had a mass of 4.80 g. After 30 minutes in a solution its mass was 4.08 g. What is the percentage change in mass?
items.e: Percentage change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100 = −0.72 ÷ 4.80 × 100. Water left by osmosis: the solution had a lower water potential.

items.q: What is the surface area to volume ratio of a block of agar measuring 4 cm × 5 cm × 10 cm?
items.e: Surface area = 220 cm²; volume = 200 mL; ratio = 220 ÷ 200. Smaller blocks have a larger ratio.

items.q: An onion cell has a water potential of −300 kPa and the salt solution has −1200 kPa. Which has the higher water potential?
items.e: The value closer to zero (−300 kPa) is higher.

items.q: Why can oxygen diffuse straight through the phospholipid bilayer?
items.e: Ions need channel proteins.

items.q: A potato strip had a mass of 4.80 g. After 30 minutes in a solution its mass was 5.28 g. What is the percentage change in mass?
items.e: Percentage change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100 = 0.48 ÷ 4.80 × 100. Water entered by osmosis: the solution had a higher water potential.

items.q: What is the surface area to volume ratio of a block of agar measuring 1 cm × 5 cm × 5 cm?
items.e: Surface area = 70 cm²; volume = 25 mL; ratio = 70 ÷ 25. Smaller blocks have a larger ratio.

items.q: What is the surface area to volume ratio of a cube of agar with sides of 4 cm?
items.e: Surface area = 96 cm²; volume = 64 mL; ratio = 96 ÷ 64. Smaller blocks have a larger ratio.

items.q: What is the surface area to volume ratio of a block of agar measuring 1 cm × 2 cm × 6 cm?
items.e: Surface area = 40 cm²; volume = 12 mL; ratio = 40 ÷ 12. Smaller blocks have a larger ratio.

items.q: What is the surface area to volume ratio of a block of agar measuring 4 cm × 5 cm × 8 cm?
items.e: Surface area = 184 cm²; volume = 160 mL; ratio = 184 ÷ 160. Smaller blocks have a larger ratio.

items.q: An onion cell has a water potential of −300 kPa and the salt solution has −1200 kPa. In which direction does water move by osmosis?
c: from the salt solution to an onion cell
from an onion cell to the salt solution
items.e: Water moves from a higher (less negative) water potential to a lower (more negative) water potential.

items.q: Cell X has a water potential of −700 kPa and cell Y has −100 kPa. Which has the higher water potential?
items.e: The value closer to zero (−100 kPa) is higher.
